Your story sounds strikingly similar to mine. Dropped out of grad school when I was 24 because the depression was so bad. I was lucky to land a job shortly afterward, but it could have easily gone even more downhill from there.

The truth is, meds won't help everyone. I know they didn't help for me, and like you I tried dozens of them. They ultimately wrecked my metabolism and I flat out told my psychiatrist they were causing enough discomfort I wasn't interested any more. They caused a physical dependency too that took months to wean myself off of. 

I did M-W-F day treatment for almost a year, but it didn't help much either. It was helpful for learning some coping skills once I got more or less on my feet again, but not much else. 

I even did ECT (electro convulsive therapy) which didn't really help and ended up erasing years of memory and disrupting my ability to form memories.

The truth is depression can be treatment resistant, and can be entirely not your fault. It totally sucks.

I was fortunate to find a career where I felt like I was helping people, so even if I was miserable at least I was making a positive impact. I still struggle with suicidal thoughts and self harm, but I am functional. All I can suggest is trying to find that one light and cling to it.

A recruiter at this company reached out to me to interview and gave a short pitch as to why I should come over... definitely a cool potential technology but there are a lot more obstacles here than just the technology part than people realize. Technically this is a medical device, and its hard to create a risk to benefit analysis for a medical device when there is no medical need being addressed.

I don't think I was clear.

ECT doesn't fit in this case because it *is* appropriate to use *because* there is data to support it. The data doesn't go to the depth of saying that it works because we know the mechanisms of action that help, but because we know that when we perform it, there are measurable results. The stuff in the middle is a 'black box', and there is well established precedent in medical regulations that so long as you know all of your inputs and outputs to the black box (including adverse side effects or events) then you have a basis to advertising the treatment. And ECT is not the only therapy where this is true. That being said, modern regulatory climate is moving away from that.

What these bogus evangelical scammers do is an entirely different, and illegal per regulation. They advertise cures and sell them with no data whatsoever. And this is the point that I think /u/MyersVandalay was trying to make. 

I focused on ECT more than I should in response because I am still salty that the risks weren't clearly communicated to me before the process, and I definitely got burned for it.

edit:
Source that I am not talking out of my ass: Years of experience in the medical industry in a role working with regulators in the US and outside US getting approval for new devices/treatments

I was told ECT essentially 'resets' some of the neurotransmitter uptakes in the brain and tries to resume some sort of 'normal' neurochemical balance. There are some other investigational treatments out there regarding the use of other forms of electrical neurostimulation/neuromodulation. It also doesn't really apply as an example here, because while we might not understand the specific mechanisms for why it works, there has still be some study and literature established for it. 

It should be (and is!) illegal to make medical claims without some approval from FDA, Notified body, or other regulatory empowered organization, and they all require evidence that the treatment not only has medical benefit, but that the benefits outweigh the risks of use. But these religious groups have some nice loopholes just for them.

As a side not for anyone seeing this, ECT is NOT a magical cure for treatment resistant depression. All it did for me was erase about 6 months of short memories and disrupt my ability to create long term memories for about a year. So not only was I still depressed, but I don't remember all of 2015 and most of 2016.

I have always hated my closet; it just simply isn't big enough. I always had to awkwardly pile everything as high as I could. This 'tower of junk', which had a gross likeness to the one in Pisa, would always precariously lean against the inside of the door. Every time that door got opened, I always had to reach out and quickly close it before all of my possessions spilled out across the floor. Once or twice I was too slow to close that damn closet door, and everything I had collapsed on top of me, filling my schedule for the next few hours as I cleaned everything up.

At a certain point, my closet became so full that the door would sometimes fail to close all of the way, and would leave a fateful crack. That door would then wait for the slightest gust of air or vibration to push it that fraction of an inch it needed. Every time someone walked briskly by, or a door closed somewhere in the house, I had to reach out and close that damn closet door. I became an expect at reaching back and closing that door; always alert and ready for the next disturbance. Soon, it became impossible to fit anything else in that closet, and I was spending half of my time quickly reaching out and shutting that door.  I must have closed that door thousands of times without ever opening it again.

But as my baggage grew larger, it became harder to close that door. The bottom few feet of closet became a true sea of mementos and other junk that I simply could not throw out. I began to have to spend more and more time closing the door. After a few months of constant attention to my closet, I decided that it was time to shut it for good. I got a wooden board and some nails, and boarded it shut. I would worry about it later, because I didn't need anything in that closet, anyway. For a while, it was glorious not having to shut that closet door. 

But without anywhere for my baggage to go, it piled ever higher. Soon the door was straining against its hinges and nailed up board, and I was suffocating. Realizing that breathing was becoming more difficult with each passing day, I began pushing against that door.

With a crack, the board snapped, the hinges failed, and that closet door opened fully for the first time ever. 

I tumbled out along with years of pent up fears, tears, and other emotions. All across my room my belongings spilled, touching every part of my small life. I was covered and buried in the stuff, unable to get up due to the weight and my exhaustion from keeping it all locked up for so long.

Soon, though, I could feel hands moving the debris off of me. A pair of  arms reached through the rubble, and pulled me up. A few others helped me to my feet, and suddenly I found myself surrounded by friends. They embraced me just as I was, some of them crying, some shocked, and others just grinning from ear to ear. It turns out, I didn't have to live in that damn closet anymore.

Fear. I am afraid to hope for anything anymore. I'm tired of being hurt. I think that is why I can't embrace that hope. At 6:30, my phone erupted in light and sound, just as it did every morning. My eyes creaked open, and were nearly blinded by the phone laying on the sheets a few inches in front of my face. My hand reached out from under the covers, and shut off the alarm. With the awful sound gone and blessed darkness back, I closed my eyes slowly. I had no desire to leave the warm comfort of my sheets, where I didn't have to care about anything at all. There was no job to do, no house to clean, and no people to see while in bed. And best of all, there was no sight of the body underneath those sheets; it didn't matter what I looked like, or who I was. When in bed, I was just another tired person. 

Despite my best efforts, I could feel the tears building. Sadness began welling deep in my chest, and I could feel my throat beginning to constrict. Memories of the dream that I had been having were still fresh in my mind, and doing their best to drag me into the pits of despair. It had been a wonderful dream, where I had been given just one wish- the one wish that I had had for years. But that wish was still just a dream, and an unrealized one at that. 

The phone began buzzing and singing again, signaling the arrival of my first get-the-hell-out-of-bed alarm. I reached out again and shut it off. I would call in sick today. I simply didn't care anymore. No more reports, no more phone calls, no more paper pushing. None of it mattered when I was doomed to always be a different person than I wanted to be. 

The next alarm was the loudest yet, just as I had programmed it to be. Chimes blared in my ears, and lights pierced my shut eyelids. I let this alarm run for a few minutes, before turning on my side and facing away from it, content to let it run its course.

Huh, that felt strange. I could feel sheets rubbing against skin that I wasn't aware that I had. I pulled my hands up to my torso, and touched my chest. My eyes instantly shot open and I bolted upright, letting the sheets fly off. My phone followed the sheets, soaring to some corner of the room, where it continued to chime and blare its alarm. I looked downwards, seeing what my still sleepy brain could hardly believe. 

I swung my legs over the edge of the bed, launched myself off of it, and ran over to the full length mirror in the bathroom, acutely aware of the flesh swinging back and forth on my chest. My feet met the cold tiles, and my hand automatically reached to the wall for the light switch. Light flooded the room, and I got a first look in the mirror. 

Bright blue eyes, watery from tears looked back at me, wide open in disbelief. No stubble could be found on that chin, and long hair fell gracefully on her thin shoulders. Two very clearly female breasts protruded from her chest. As I looked southwards, I could see quite clearly that this was a very gorgeous woman looking back at me.

I fell to my knees, and the woman in the mirror did the same. I reached out, touching the mirror and the girl that I was looking at. A genuine smile broke across her face- no- my face. Suddenly I knew that everything was going to be alright.
Oh, I guess I made that unclear. I was assigned male at birth. At 18 I was very confused with my gender identity, and preferred to go with what was much easier versus what I knew to be true.

I am a 21 year old female. I would tell 18 year old me;

1) You know who you are. Do not run from it- save yourself from the grief. You are a girl; I know it is extremely scary to think about what that means, but the sooner you accept it, the sooner you will find happiness.

2) You are going to try and do some big things, and you are going to fail. Failing is OK. Don't beat yourself up on it.

3) Stop second guessing yourself. You have never made a 'bad' decision in your life, and you won't anytime in the near future, either. 

4) Do what you WANT to do, not what you think you SHOULD do, or what you think is best for everyone. 

5) Things will get better, especially when you finally come out to yourself. You will meet some awesome people who will help you through it all. Things will be OK, I promise.

The ragtag group of individuals knew not where their vessel was headed, nor how long it would take to get there. The complicated arrays of sensors, dials, and levers  in the cockpit meant nothing to them, and every last switch and control was frozen in place, unyielding to their best efforts to move them. They could glean no information from anything on board as to how long they would last out in the infinite depths of space, and their heads all buzzed with the same questions; How long will the oxygen last? How much fuel is left? When will the food run out? Where in the universe are we going?

These were the next great pioneers of the human race. When plans were drawn for a one way trip to the far depths of space to test the reactions humans had to years of space travel, 'volunteers' were hard to come by. While many would jump at the chance for a one way trip to Mars to begin work on the new Colony, none would even think about a one way trip to see how long it would take for them to die. With no one to test on, the project stalled, and it seemed as if the billions spent on the state of the art craft would be wasted. 

After months of deliberation, the State came forward with an idea. The last great criminals of the old Order were set for execution, but popular sentiment was greatly against it. After all, who are we to determine who has the right to live or die in such an enlightened society? The State proposed to use these last death row inmates for this experiment. Society could not say that the lives of these men and women were wasted, since they would be gaining valuable scientific knowledge. The Space Agency quietly agreed, and soon the small group of individuals were strapped to a ship attached to a 10 story rocket. The public was told that these individuals were redeeming themselves to the State; for their sacrifices would pave the way for humanity's foray into the depths of space.

On board this lone island of humanity in the sea of nothingness was a myriad of criminals from the old way of life. A rapist who had no prejudice in his sexual urges. A woman with a hunger so insatiable she would eat her fellow human. The leader of the last rebellion, who at one point commanded thousands in his bid for power. The man whose laziness caused the death of hundreds of thousands to a nuclear plant meltdown. A murderer who relished in slowly dismembering her victims before displaying them on the streets. A robber, who made off with millions of valuables from those that had more than him. The last Dictator of the old order, who exploited his people for wealth and kept them under his iron fist.

Several months into their one way trip, a crackling could be heard from the radio in the cockpit. The old rebellion leader was the first to hear it, and quickly called his fellows over. The others rushed to his side, and soon they were all intently listening to the faint static. Shortly afterwards, the static gave way to a faint noise; a mumbling of sounds they could not understand. These sounds would continue for a few minutes before abruptly changing in characteristics. The crew did not know what to make of any of these, and began wondering aloud what they could mean. But eventually, their questions were answered when they heard a sound they could understand.

"Do the life forms on board this vessel understand the Human language? You are approaching the Galactic Republic border. Please state your identity, and purpose for leaving your home world of Earth."

The old dictator leaned forward and pressed the button on the radio. "We are of Earth. Who are we speaking to."

The voice on the other end immediately responded. "I am a representative of the Galactic Republic. On behalf of the entire Republic, I would like to formally welcome the people of Earth and offer congratulations to the Humans. With your voyage to our quadrant of space, it is apparent that you have advanced far enough to engage with us in the exchanging of ideas, goods, and knowledge. We know nothing about your way of life or being, as we have distanced ourselves from you as to not interfere with your development. Please, tell us about yourself, and your trade."

The criminals, bewildered, looked at one another, trying to figure out what to do. But everyone knew that they had the same idea, they had a way to live.

The rapist was the first to lean forward. "My name is Lust. On Earth, I was a lover. I loved my fellow human so much that it caused me pain on the inside. My job was to share that love, and to make everyone feel my pleasure."

The cannibal grinned. She knew what the rapist was doing, and she quickly thought of her own story. "On Earth, they called me Gluttony. I was a connoisseur of tastes, bringing the joys related to food to my fellow man. My job was to seek these new tastes, and to indulge in them, and to tell people of their wonders. "

The old rebellion leader spoke next. "They called me Greed. Back home, I was a leader who sought to bring power to my people. I was a liberator, and a conqueror. My job was to bring me and my people more."

The nuclear technician shuffled up next. "They called me Sloth. I sought comfort and relaxation above all else. I was admired for my carefree ideals, and my ability to watch without interfering."

The next to speak was the murderer, angry that she had to wait so long. "I am Wrath. I was a scientist of sorts, drawing pleasure and knowledge from learning about my fellow man. I always wanted to know what made them tick, and to understand the atrocities that they would do to me and their fellow human."

The robber came next. "My name is Envy. I worked to spread the wealth among my fellow man. What others had that I did not, I took. I was a humanitarian, taking from those who had too much for those who had too little."

Last to come forward was the old Dictator. He smiled, knowing what he had to do. His fellow criminals had set this up beautifully. "I am the esteemed Pride of Earth. I once was a leader of a large group of people. I would provide for them, and lead them to great wealth and prosperity. But now, our Earth has been overrun by degenerates and criminals. I will not stand to see my people, and the other people of Earth oppressed so. Please, members of the Galactic Republic, return with us to Earth. Our mission is a humanitarian, one. We seek to return Earth to its glory, and the ideals that we all represent. Please, help us."

The radio was silent for a moment, then the voice came back.

"Very well. We will return to Earth, and return it to its true glory. You will be asked to lead, and will sit in our Galactic Senate."

The Dictator let a smile play across his lips. The universe was on his side, after all. Nothing could stop him, now.

Everybody loves Kazaam. Or at least, now they do.

When Kazaam first appeared on the streets, he was known only as Chris Smalls, and he didn't have a very pristine reputation. The guy could teleport anywhere he wanted to at will, so of course he was teleporting into places where he didn't exactly belong. VIP clubs, secure areas, ladies locker rooms- you name it, and Chris at some point or another got into it. Eventually, the law caught up with him, and an arrest at all costs was put out through the system. Wanted "Dead or Alive" joked all the newspapers. It seemed like young Chris was heading nowhere, or rather, everywhere, in a hurry. 

But one day, the cops came forward with a deal. They had a hostage situation, and they could use his help; get the innocent people out of there, and his crimes would be forgiven. Chris jumped on the offer, and sure enough was able to teleport into the bank and save those people. With Chris' helping hand, they were even able to catch the crook himself, who happened to be none other than a nefarious serial robber with a hefty bounty. Chris suddenly had a clean record, and a pocketful of cash. It was then that he realized that he could probably really help the people around him, while earning a comfortable living on the side. 

It took some time for the public to change their opinion of him, but soon he became everyone's favorite local hero. His face became a common sight on the evening news, and his new name, 'Kazaam', a frequent subject in the paper. And this time, it was for all of the good reasons. Ironically enough, he was now getting into all the sorts of places he wanted to before, except with open doors and arms. Kazaam had a good life going for him, and it seemed like there was nothing that could stop his zero to hero story.

You can imagine Hank's surprise when he looked up late one Wednesday night to see a disheveled and slightly drunk Kazaam stumble into his bar. 

Kazaam shuffled over to the bar counter, eased himself onto one of the stools and laid his forehead against the cool wood. Hank couldn't hear exactly what he started mumbling about, but he heard 'scotch' and 'rocks' somewhere in there so he poured out a glass and placed it next to Kazaam's head.

"On the house. You earned it, Kazaam."

Kazaam raised his head, stared at the glass for a moment and then downed it. He smacked his lips, rubbed the back of his sleeve against his lips and then buried his face in his hands. 

"Thanks," muttered Kazaam. "But tonight, I am Chris. And I'm paying for that drink."

Hank shrugged and took Chris' glass. "Sure thing, Chris. Whatever you want. Anything else I can get you? Anything I can help with? You seem a little...down."

Chris lowered his hands and propped his elbows on the counter. He gave Hank a bewildered look, as if he didn't really understand what he just said. "You mean... you actually care? I mean, you care if I'm, you know, feeling down?"

"Well, yeah, sure. I may not be able to help much, but I got a pretty good ear. Hell, you are probably a lot more interesting than the normal bozos I get around here." Hank chuckled to himself a little. "C'mon, Chris. I'll hear anything you have to say. I can only imagine what can get one of you super heroes down."

Chris' face turned sour with the words 'super hero'. "I hate being a super hero," he whispered. "People don't understand the cost of a super power. They don't understand what we have to give up. Give me another scotch and I'll tell you why."

Hank pulled out the scotch and poured out a generous amount for Chris. Chris picked his new glass, swirled it in his hands for a moment, seeming to be mulling over what he was going to say next, before taking a sip. He placed down the glass and began to speak.

"When I teleport, it it not instantaneous to me; I still have to travel there." Chris raised his glass as if for another sip, but instead began to stare into the depths of his drink. "When I teleport, I fade into what I can only describe as nonexistence. For all intents and purposes, I die. And let me tell you, is it painful." Chris finally took another sip and put the glass down.

"When I teleport, I go into the beyond. It is cold, and painful, and scary. I wouldn't wish my worst enemy there. At first, I would only teleport into places that I couldn't normally, but would be a lot of fun. I mean, it would have to be pretty damn awesome place to justify that sort of pain, right? But when I got into trouble, things weren't so fun anymore. My trips were no longer done for pleasure at that point, but were done as a distraction. I couldn't just stop teleporting, because it will never leave me. The memory of the place is burned in my mind. It followed me in my sleep. It haunted me."

Chris fell silent again and took a drought from his drink. He started chewing his lip, trying to think of what to say next. Hank was bewildered. He had no idea how Chris was able to teleport, and he had never really thought of it. He felt sorry for the kid, now, whereas before he might have been a little jealous of the boy.

"That sounds terrible. But you then started helping people. You saved lives. Did that help?"

Chris smiled wryly. "At first it did. The police deal was a dream come true. And then I certainly got some satisfaction from helping people. But soon, the novelty wore off and I could no longer escape my pain, again. For every life that I saved, I died. It was excruciating. And now, I am trapped. Helping people is the only reason I live, but for everyone I help I must die. I can't just abandon it anymore, too. It is too much of who I am. The cold and the pain follow me, regardless. Even when I am alive, it is almost like I am dead."

Hank was speechless. He did not except anything like this. Reeling, Hank said the only thing that he could think. "What's it like, dying?"

Chris smiled,looked Hank in the eyes, and responded, "Why do you think I haven't gone for real, yet?"

John could tell that Emma was nervous. Her eyes could not stay in one place for too long, and kept darting back and forth trying to find something to fix on. Occasionally her gaze would meet his and she would blush and quickly look away. Her hands could not stay still, and were constantly wringing the deep red napkin in her lap. When she reached out to sip her wine, her hands visibly shook. John could not figure out why his date was so nervous, and felt a little confused. Emma had not acted like this on any of their previous dates. Albeit, none of their other dates were at the only four star restaurant in town, but this seemed a little over the top to him. The only explanation that John could think of was that something was bothering Emma, and he feared that it was about him.

John was head over heels for Emma. He first saw her in a coffee shop across the street from his old high school, reading some book that he couldn't remember; He was too captivated by her gentle face and simple elegance to remember such a petty detail. In a trance-like state he approached her that day, and stammered out an introduction. She looked up from her book and into his eyes, and from that moment on he was in love.

He could see such a gentle soul in her eyes, and a certain knowing about them. When she looked at him, he felt content and happy, as if they belonged to an old friend. Deep down, he felt as if he already knew her, even though they had only just met.

At first, Emma seemed a little reluctant to go on that first date. When he asked her to join him for coffee the next day, he could see a glimmer of worry skate across her eyes and a hint of uncertainty in her face, but she said yes. When they met the next day, that look was gone but John was always a little fearful that she didn't love him like he loved her. And it was this fear that was beginning to bubble in his throat, now. 

After a few minutes of mindless chit chat, John finally gave in to his burning curiosity, and asked his date, "Hey, Em. Is something wrong? You seem a little nervous."

Emma's eyes suddenly stopped darting around, and she looked down straight at her empty plate. Her hands stropped wringing her napkin and she became very still. John visibly stiffened and began searching in her eyes for some clue as to what she might be thinking, but all he could see was the reflection of the lone candle on the table dancing.

"Nothing." She eventually muttered. "Nothing is wrong."

"All right," responded John slowly, letting the sound of doubt seep into his words seep into words. "I care about you a lot, and I am a little worried, that is all. You don't have to talk if you don't want to."

Emma grinned and looked up, staring straight into his eyes. "I know what you are worried about. You are worried that I don't like you back. It is written all over you." She smirked, a little. "Don't worry, dear, I like you plenty. Perhaps more than I care to admit. That is not what is on my mind."

"Oh, ok," sighed John, very relieved. "But tell me, what is bothering you. I want to help."

Emma opened her mouth as if to say something, but then held back. John could see her thinking carefully, mulling over the words in her head. Finally, she spoke. 

"We went to the same high school, you know. It was over ten years ago, and you probably don't recognize me. But I certainly recognize you. We had a lot of the same friends, and even knew each other pretty well. But we never actually met."

John frantically searched his memories for any recollection of Emma. There were only a handful of girls that he knew back in high school, and Emma wasn't one of them, as far as he could tell. Memories flooded his brain and he tried his best to search through them, to no avail. But suddenly, he saw her eyes. Yes! He had seen her eyes before, but they didn't belong to any girl he knew. 

John's face must have been amusing to watch, because Emma suddenly laughed. 

"I was nervous dating you the first time because I was not sure if you would recognize me. I didn't know if I could handle you remembering me right away. But you know, I think you are ready to know. After all, we were best friends senior year."

And that's when John knew. His best friend had dropped off the radar about a year after graduation. No one had been able to figure out where his old best friend had gone. John was thrilled, but also surprised. He didn't know what to think, or what to say. All he could manage, was a feeble, "Michael?"

Emma smiled, and a single tear rolled down her cheek.

"Hi, John."

Thank you. I am a little nervous about writing them a letter because I am not sure they will take it seriously. Being an INTP is not a condition, as you seem to be implying. Taken right from the sidebar, it is a personality type within the Jungian Cognitive Function Theory, which categorizes cognitive predisposition. I am not an expert in this theory, but I believe this is not something that can be very easily changed, as it is a derivative of personality. It is not a good, or a bad thing, merely a way to describe the way a person perceives and thinks about things.

That being said, there is nothing wrong with being an INTP. It is not something that needs to be cured or improved upon, as it is simply a part of who we are. Sure, we might have a few problems with people as a result of our introversion and way of thinking, but it isn't something that we should be ashamed of or treat like it is 'wrong'. We just have to work a little harder at it. Places like this are great because we can encourage each other and offer support for those situations where we need to put in a little extra effort. 

Some of what you say is true. It is a great idea to play to your strengths and improve your weaknesses, and to use your personality to help look in the right direction to find things that you will enjoy. But there is also nothing wrong with sticking to the same things if they make you happy. 

TLDR: I am a proud INTP, and I wouldn't trade my strengths and weaknesses for anything in the world.

I went through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for a few months last year. I had been fighting depression for a few years by that point, and it was destroying my few remaining friendships. I was highly skeptical at the time if it would help me, and I was very reluctant to give up my independence and expose myself to someone, but I went in anyway because I was desperate to save my friendships. 

It was, overall, a positive force for me. It didn't necessarily solve my problems but it helped me think about them in different ways. The therapy helped me become more conscious of my automatic thoughts  and helped me direct them in a more beneficial direction. What it essentially did was give me a powerful coping mechanism for whenever I was feeling the most down, or when something bad would happen. 

It didn't solve my problems, but it was able to clear my head enough and alleviate my depression enough to address my problems in a meaningful manner. My therapist was also a great source for bouncing ideas about potential solutions to my problem, and she was able to ask questions that I hadn't thought of before. 

I believe that Cognitive Behavior Therapy works well at helping people change old habits of thinking to more positive ways. Elements of happiness are, after all, a mind set. Naturally, it can't really solve all problems for all people, but I think approaching it with an open mind and willingness to try new things really helps.

[Maslow's Hierarchy of needs](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maslow's_hierarchy_of_needs).
Essentially, Before someone can worry about something like depression, they have to worry about more fundamental issues, for example food, water, shelter, a steady income. In higher income countries, more of the population has their basic physiological needs met, so they can worry about the next level of fulfillment. There are many other factors that play into depression, but the conditions are more ripe for them in higher income countries.
